steps.body:
Instead of y as a function of x, let BOTH coordinates depend on a third variable — the **parameter** t, often time:

x = x(t),  y = y(t).

As t advances, the point (x(t), y(t)) traces a curve. This can draw shapes no single y = f(x) can — loops, circles, paths that double back.

widget.prompt: For x = t + 1, y = 2t, where is the point at t = 2? Enter its y-coordinate.

commonErrors.feedback: y = 2t = 2·2 = 4 (you may have used t itself). The x-coordinate is 3; the y is 4.
3 is the x-coordinate (t + 1). The y-coordinate is 2t = 4.

steps.body: Drag the point forward along the path.

widget.prompt: For x = t + 1, y = 2t, drag the point forward and watch which way the arrows point.
widget.successFeedback: At t = 2 the point has reached (3, 4) — every arrow along the way pointed up and to the right, because both coordinates grow as t grows.
widget.lowFeedback: Not far enough yet — keep dragging forward; t is still short of 2.
widget.highFeedback: Too far — you've dragged past t = 2. Bring it back a little.

explanationVariants: As t increases, both x = t + 1 and y = 2t increase — the point moves up and to the right.
Larger t → larger x and larger y: motion toward the upper right.

widget.prompt: For x = t + 1, y = 2t, as t increases the point moves:

options.label: up and to the right
options.feedback: Right — both coordinates grow with t, so the traced direction is up-right.

options.label: down and to the left
options.feedback: Both x and y INCREASE with t (positive coefficients), so the motion is up-right.

options.label: in a circle
options.feedback: Linear-in-t coordinates trace a straight LINE, not a circle. Here it heads up-right.

steps.body: The same shape can be traced at different **speeds** or **directions** depending on the parametrization. x = cos t, y = sin t draws the unit circle counterclockwise from (1, 0); x = cos t, y = −sin t draws the SAME circle clockwise. The curve is the trail; the parametrization is the journey.
Drag the point a quarter turn and watch which way it swings.

widget.prompt: x = cos t, y = sin t starts at (1, 0). Drag the point forward to t = π/2 and watch which way it turns.
widget.successFeedback: At t = π/2 the point has swung up to (0, 1) — counterclockwise the whole way, which is the standard direction for increasing t on the unit circle.
widget.lowFeedback: Not far enough yet — keep dragging forward around the circle.
widget.highFeedback: Too far — you've swept past t = π/2. Bring it back a little.

explanationVariants: x = cos t, y = sin t: at t = 0 it's at (1, 0); at t = π/2 it's at (0, 1) — moving counterclockwise.
Rising from (1,0) up to (0,1) is the counterclockwise direction.

widget.prompt: x = cos t, y = sin t starts at (1, 0). At t = π/2 it reaches (0, 1), so it travels:

options.label: clockwise
options.feedback: Clockwise would go (1,0) → (0,−1). Here it rises to (0,1): counterclockwise.

options.label: back and forth on a line
options.feedback: Sine and cosine together trace a CIRCLE, and this one goes counterclockwise.

explanationVariants: x = t², y = t: at t = ±1 both give x = 1 but y = ±1 — two points share an x, so it's not a function of x, yet parametric form handles it fine.
The sideways parabola fails the vertical line test but is an easy parametric curve.

widget.prompt: Why can x = t², y = t trace a curve that's NOT a function y = f(x)?

options.label: Two t-values share x but give different y-values.
options.feedback: Right — x = 1 pairs with both y = 1 and y = −1; parametric form allows it.

options.label: Squaring t makes x nonnegative, not multivalued.
options.feedback: True that x ≥ 0, but the real reason it's not a function is the repeated x with two y-values.

options.label: It passes the vertical-line test as one y for each x.
options.feedback: It fails the vertical line test: x = 1 has y = ±1. Parametric curves needn't be functions.

explanationVariants: x = 2cos t, y = 2sin t at t = π: x = 2cos π = −2, y = 2sin π = 0. The point is (−2, 0); its x-coordinate is −2.
Half a turn around a radius-2 circle lands on the negative x-axis at (−2, 0).
hints: Substitute t = π into both equations.

widget.prompt: For x = 2cos t, y = 2sin t, what is the x-coordinate at t = π?

commonErrors.feedback: 0 is the y-coordinate (2sin π). The x-coordinate is 2cos π = −2.

takeaways: Parametric form: x = x(t), y = y(t); the point traces a curve as t moves.
Direction and speed depend on the parametrization, not just the shape.
Parametric curves can violate the vertical line test — loops and doubling-back are fine.
steps.teaser: Next: erasing t to recover a familiar x-y equation.

concept.body: Parametric: substitute a t-value into x(t) and y(t) to get the point at that instant. Increasing t traces the curve in a definite direction.

widget.prompt: For x = 3t, y = t − 1, what is x at t = 2?

commonErrors.feedback: 1 is y = t − 1. The x-coordinate is 3t = 6.
